comparison: Both evaluate the sliding model using overlapping evidence (C2, C20-C21, C30-C39). OpenEval finds the evidence convincing with multiple converging lines supporting 1D diffusion. Peer reviewers acknowledge the evidence is 'strong' but raise major concerns that the interpretation assumes coaxial rod geometry and ignores possible off-axis motion (swinging/fluctuations), requesting discussion of how this may affect interpretations and simulations.

Both assess homology detection during sliding (C3, C7-C8, C40-C51, C57-C59). OpenEval finds the evidence convincing based on FRET transitions, HMM analysis, and control experiments. Peer reviewers question whether the 5-nucleotide distance between HS1 and HS2 is sufficient to conclude transitions are due to sliding versus alternative mechanisms, requesting additional evidence.

Both evaluate whether orientation flipping occurs (C56). OpenEval finds control experiments (Figure 4 supplement 4) rule out flipping. Peer reviewers suggest statistical analysis is needed to determine orientation fractions and whether reorientation occurs, proposing a modified assay to test if both sites can be recognized in a single binding event.

Both address the diffusion coefficient measurement (C4, C52). OpenEval finds it well-supported by cross-correlation analysis and Monte Carlo simulations. Peer reviewers' concern about off-axis motion affecting 'data interpretations and simulations' extends to these quantitative measurements, since they depend on coaxial rod geometry assumptions.

Both evaluate the search length calculation (C5, C53). OpenEval finds it well-supported by combining measured diffusion coefficient with observed dissociation times. Peer reviewers' uncertainty about the diffusion coefficient accuracy (due to off-axis motion concerns) propagates to this derived quantity.

Both assess the 200-fold enhancement claim and functional implications (C6, C54-C55, C60-C61). OpenEval marks uncertain due to unknown microscopic rate constants and model-dependent predictions. Peer reviewers' uncertainty stems from concerns about the validity of the underlying sliding model and diffusion measurements, which affect downstream modeling.

Both evaluate background claims and established context (C1, C10-C19). OpenEval finds these well-established with appropriate citations. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this framework by stating the work is 'of significant interest and high quality' and 'a significant advance' without questioning the background.

Both assess electrostatic interaction characterization (C23-C28). OpenEval finds strong support from salt dependence, mutant validation, and ATP independence. Peer reviewers do not raise concerns about these characterization experiments, focusing instead on interpretation of fluctuations as linear sliding.

Both evaluate the novelty claim (C9). OpenEval supports it based on experimental demonstration combined with literature comparison. Peer reviewers implicitly support this by stating results 'represent a significant advance of the current understanding' without challenging the novelty claim.

Both address speculation about Rad51 and prior work context (C62-C63). OpenEval notes appropriate qualification as speculation. Peer reviewers do not challenge this discussion point as it does not affect main conclusions about RecA.

Both evaluate functional implications for reorganization (C60-C61). OpenEval finds these well-supported inferences from demonstrated sliding and homology detection. Peer reviewers' uncertainty about the sliding model validity and transition mechanisms propagates to these functional interpretations.

OpenEval evaluates reduced recognition at HS1 terminal position (C48) as supported by experimental data. This claim appears in peer R2 which addresses homology detection; peer reviewers' uncertainty about transition mechanisms between sites relates to but does not directly challenge the terminal position observation.
